# RG14 `dependent-precondition`: The attack depends on another party acting

<!-- Generated by `realism-gate explain --markdown`. Do not edit by hand. -->

**Severity:** note (note)

realism.yaml declares a precondition performed by the victim, a privileged role or a third party.

## Why it matters

This is not a defect, it is a fact the severity argument has to carry. An attack that needs a victim to deposit, a keeper to harvest or governance to vote is real, but it is conditional, and triagers price conditional attacks below unconditional ones. The note keeps the dependency visible in the output.

## How to fix it

Name the dependency in the report's attack requirements and argue how likely it is.

## Does not fire on

```yaml
  - step: a user deposits into the empty vault
    performed_by: victim
    boundary: own_transaction
```

## How it can be wrong

None known. This rule reads a declaration you wrote, not your code.

## In Solana tests (Rust and Anchor TypeScript)

The same: the rule reads `realism.yaml`, whatever language the tests are written in.

## In Move tests (Sui and Aptos)

Not checked. Move unit tests have no Foundry cheatcode and this rule reads one, or it reads realism.yaml on its own. Privileged signers, admin caps, test-only mints, missing assertions and missing baselines are the Move checks.

## Silencing it

An `allow` comment in the repo under review does not silence this rule, and neither does a `realism.yaml` or `realism-gate.toml` inside that repo. Policy is an operator file outside the tree (`--declaration`, `--config`). `--trust-inline-allows` is the author switch, for a PoC you wrote and are not gating.

```solidity
// realism-gate: allow(RG14) <why this is not a defect here>
```

The comment is the same in Rust, TypeScript and Move. A comment without a reason is ignored even with `--trust-inline-allows`, and the output says so.
